deep.intro: Weights walk out, or behavior is copied through the front door. They share almost no controls, and programs that plan for one usually have nothing for the other.

blocks.body: Exfiltration from storage, training infrastructure, backups, or an endpoint, usually via credentials rather than intrusion. The loss is total and permanent, because a model cannot be rotated the way a key can, and the 2023 LLaMA leak remains the demonstration.
blocks.label: Weights leave

blocks.body: Systematic querying of the API to train a substitute model. Nothing is breached, every request is individually legitimate, and the theft exists only in the aggregate pattern, which is why it is a detection problem rather than an access-control one.
blocks.label: Behavior is copied

deep.heading: The two theft paths

blocks.body: The most direct path, established by federal charges against a former Google engineer accused of taking AI trade secrets. Access legitimately held is the hardest vector to distinguish from work.
blocks.label: Insider exfiltration

blocks.body: Cloud keys, CI systems, notebooks, and orchestration platforms with standing access to weight storage. RAND's published analysis of frontier-weight security catalogues these vectors in detail.
blocks.label: Credential and infrastructure compromise

blocks.body: Copies that inherit none of the controls placed on the primary store, which is where custody programs most often break in practice.
blocks.label: Backup and snapshot exposure

blocks.body: Weights on laptops and shared drives for convenience during development, each copy a new custody boundary nobody assessed.
blocks.label: Endpoint sprawl

blocks.body: High-volume structured querying to train a copycat, which moved from academic concern to commercial dispute in 2025 when providers publicly alleged rivals had trained on their outputs against terms.
blocks.label: API distillation

blocks.body: Rebuilding capability from generated content collected at scale, including through intermediaries, so no single account shows the sweep.
blocks.label: Functional reconstruction from outputs

deep.intro: Weights deserve the threat model of code-signing keys, not of ordinary data. The controls below reflect that.

blocks.body: Hold weight access to a short list of named roles, enforce hardware-backed authentication, and treat every access as a logged security event rather than routine work.
blocks.label: Named-role access with hardware MFA

blocks.body: Encrypt at rest with hardware-backed keys, and separate key custody from model custody so no single compromise yields both.
blocks.label: Encryption and key custody

blocks.body: Constrain and monitor every route weights can travel, including backups and snapshots. Exfiltration needs a channel, and this is the layer that closes it.
blocks.label: Egress control on the storage path

blocks.body: No full weight copies on endpoints or general-purpose buckets, with automated detection of copies outside approved stores.
blocks.label: Copy discipline

blocks.body: Baseline legitimate API use and hunt sweep signatures: systematic input-space coverage, deterministic probing, distillation-shaped prompt distributions, and coordinated low-and-slow activity across accounts.
blocks.label: Extraction-pattern detection

blocks.body: Rate limits and quotas that make wholesale extraction uneconomical, tiered capability exposure, and terms enforcement with real consequence.
blocks.label: Commercial controls

blocks.body: Pin custody, access, and breach-notification duties contractually on any provider holding your fine-tuned weights, since their controls are now your exposure.
blocks.label: Vendor custody obligations

deep.heading: Custody controls for the crown jewels

blocks.body: What is our most valuable model worth, and is it protected like that number or like a file? Who can read the weights today, and would we see it if they did? Do backups and snapshots carry the same controls as the primary store? Could we detect a systematic extraction campaign against our API, and what would we do about it? If a fine-tuned model of ours sat with a vendor, what does the contract oblige them to do, and have we verified it? The distinguishing question: a stolen credential can be rotated, and stolen weights cannot, so does our response plan acknowledge that this loss is permanent?
blocks.label: Questions worth asking about model custody

deep.heading: What to ask about model custody

deep.intro: Distillation, training a smaller model on a stronger model's outputs, is a legitimate technique. In September 2026 the US government and Anthropic separately documented it being done covertly and at industrial scale, through fake accounts, stolen credentials and proxy networks. The figures below are Anthropic's, for its own models only; the government advisory covers Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok and gives no per-company counts.

blocks.body: On 8 September 2026 the NSA, CISA and FBI named six China-based companies, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI, as extracting billions of tokens across millions of exchanges from US frontier models since at least late 2024, likely with Chinese government awareness. The agencies call distillation the critical core of these companies' development strategy, not a supplement to it.
blocks.label: The government finding

blocks.body: The largest distillation attack Anthropic says it has measured: over 151 million exchanges between May and July 2026, peaking near 3 million a day from more than 3,500 fraudulent accounts. A fixed prompt forced Claude Opus to write out its reasoning, which was converted into fine-tuning data for Qwen 3.5, 3.6 and 3.7.
blocks.label: Alibaba (Qwen)

blocks.body: Over 23 million exchanges between May and July 2026. Anthropic found Moonshot silently forwarded its own customers' requests to Claude and showed them Claude's answers as Kimi's: almost 300,000 requests in one ten-day period, through 5,380 fraudulent accounts. The relayed traffic included a user Anthropic assesses was likely PLA-affiliated, analyzing CCTV footage of one person.
blocks.label: Moonshot AI (Kimi)

blocks.body: Over 12.1 million exchanges in 14 days in July 2026. Like Moonshot, it relayed some of its own users' requests to Claude Opus without telling them, and replayed Claude's reasoning signatures in new sessions to recover reasoning Claude would otherwise have summarized.
blocks.label: DeepSeek

blocks.body: Zhipu: over 3.4 million exchanges in 17 days, including an attempt to distill cyber capabilities that it abandoned against Anthropic's strongest model and moved to weaker ones. Xiaomi: over 400,000 exchanges, replaying its own users' sessions through Claude. SenseTime bought harvested Claude transcripts from third-party vendors; MiniMax ran its own proxy service through an undisclosed shell company.
blocks.label: Zhipu (Z.ai), Xiaomi, SenseTime and MiniMax

blocks.body: The access layer behind all of it: gray-market API proxies that create thousands of accounts with false identities, fake or stolen cards and stolen API keys to get around geographic restrictions. Many also log their users' exchanges and sell them. Both the advisory and Anthropic name them.
blocks.label: Transfer stations

blocks.body: Anthropic reports that a model distilled from a frontier model can gain dangerous capabilities, including in the biological and cyber domains, even when the harvested exchanges say little about those subjects, and that the original model's safeguards do not carry over. The relayed traffic also exposed users' names, company data and live credentials to a third party without their knowledge.
blocks.label: Why it matters beyond competition

deep.heading: Industrial-scale distillation: the 2026 record

deep.intro: The two sources recommend overlapping defenses, and they describe what each provider can do alone and what only works together.

blocks.body: Anthropic attributes proxy account activity to the organization behind it and acts against the whole network instead of banning accounts one at a time.
blocks.label: Attribute, do not whack-a-mole

blocks.body: The advisory: watch for anomalous prompts, accounts and networks, subscription-to-usage ratios out of line, new accounts at maximum usage immediately, and enterprise-scale throughput. Anthropic: classifiers built specifically to detect adversarial extraction.
blocks.label: Detect the pattern

blocks.body: Claude summarizes its internal reasoning before responding, and preserved thinking in Fable 5.1 stops new API accounts from editing the context that precedes the model's reasoning, a common way to make it reveal that reasoning.
blocks.label: Protect the reasoning

blocks.body: The advisory recommends subtly altering responses to suspected distillers, so harvested data is worth less.
blocks.label: Degrade the payoff

blocks.body: Anthropic can require identity verification from accounts showing abuse signals, such as unauthorized resale or operation from unsupported countries, and bans accounts that fail it.
blocks.label: Verify identity

blocks.body: The advisory: correlate activity across model providers, cloud platforms and API aggregators, because campaigns are deliberately spread so no single provider sees the whole of it.
blocks.label: Share across providers

topic.body: Model theft is the loss of the model itself: weights exfiltrated from storage or infrastructure, or the model's behavior extracted through its own API by systematic querying that trains a copycat, distillation without permission. Weights concentrate enormous value, training investment, embedded data, and capability, into files an insider or intruder can copy in minutes, and unlike a stolen password the loss is unrecoverable: once out, the model is out forever. Extraction through the API is subtler, no breach occurs, every query is individually legitimate, and the theft is only visible in the aggregate pattern.

Both branches are documented. The most prominent weights case is the leak of Meta's LLaMA weights in 2023, distributed publicly within days of limited research release, and criminal indictments of insiders exfiltrating AI trade secrets from major labs, including a former Google engineer charged federally, established the insider path. Security analyses of frontier-weight theft, notably RAND's published attack-vector taxonomy, catalogue dozens of routes from credential theft to infrastructure compromise. On the extraction side, academic work has long shown functionality-stealing against commercial APIs, and the distillation disputes of 2025, providers publicly alleging rivals trained on their outputs against terms, moved API extraction from research concern to commercial incident.

For weights: treat access as a monitored event, not a permission. Alert on bulk reads of weight storage, unusual snapshot or export operations, copies to endpoints or external buckets, and any access outside the small named set of roles with a reason to touch them. Egress monitoring on the storage path is the tripwire that catches exfiltration in progress. For extraction: baseline legitimate API usage and hunt sweep patterns, high-volume systematically structured queries covering input space, distinctive temperature-zero probing, distillation-style prompt distributions, and coordinated low-and-slow querying across accounts. Watermarking and output-fingerprinting research offers after-the-fact attribution, but pattern detection is the practical control today.

Custody discipline for weights: encrypted storage, hardware-backed keys, access held to a handful of named roles with hardware MFA, no full copies on laptops or shared buckets, and egress controls on every path weights can travel, the threat model of code-signing keys, not ordinary data. For the API: rate limits and quotas that make wholesale extraction uneconomical, terms enforcement with teeth, tiered capability exposure so the free tier does not give away the product, and query auditing wired to the sweep-pattern detection above. Contractually pin custody obligations on every provider holding your fine-tuned weights, and put weight custody on the risk register as the crown-jewel entry it is.

domains.body: For a frontier lab the weights are the crown jewels, and for any enterprise with a fine-tuned model they are a concentrated asset carrying training investment and embedded data. Governance treats weight custody as a named risk: where copies live, who can export them, and what contractual protections cover the providers holding them. Published security frameworks from the labs themselves, and independent analyses of weight-theft attack vectors, give the register real content, including the insider and infrastructure paths that matter more than exotic attacks.
domains.label: Security Governance and Risk Management

domains.body: Weight protection is infrastructure discipline: encrypted storage, hardware-backed key custody, tightly scoped access with hardware MFA for the handful of roles that genuinely need it, egress monitoring on the storage paths where weights live, and no full copies on laptops or in shared buckets. The threat model resembles code-signing key protection more than ordinary data security, because a single successful exfiltration is unrecoverable.
domains.label: Architecture and Engineering

domains.body: Extraction through the API is theft without a breach: systematic querying can distill a deployed model's behavior into a clone, no weights required. Providers defend with rate limits, query auditing, and terms enforcement, and product teams exposing their own models publicly should assume distillation attempts and decide deliberately how much capability the free tier reveals.
domains.label: Application and Product Security

domains.body: Extraction has a signature: high-volume, systematically structured queries that sweep input space rather than serve users. Operations teams for exposed model endpoints should baseline legitimate usage and alert on sweep patterns, the same anomaly discipline applied to credential stuffing, aimed at a newer target.
domains.label: Security Operations
